questions.question: Which of the following best describes a chemical system that is in equilibrium?
questions.answer: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates.
options: The concentrations of the reactants and products are the same
The rate of conversion of reactants to products is minimal
The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are the same

questions.question: Atomic absorption spectroscopy uses the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum. Which regions are used by (I) NMR, (II) colourimetry and (III) IR spectroscopy, in that order?
questions.answer: NMR uses radio waves, colourimetry visible light and IR spectroscopy infrared.

questions.question: Nylon is a condensation polymer made from hexanedioic acid and 1,6-diaminohexane. Which type of linkage is present in nylon?
questions.answer: A carboxylic acid and an amine condense to form an amide link.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
questions.answer: The longest chain has six carbons; numbering gives the lowest locants, 3,3,4.

questions.question: Consider the equilibrium in a closed container at 350 °C: $$\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2(g)\quad\Delta H=-85\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: Cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction.
options: Decreasing the temperature will increase the amount of SO$_2$Cl$_2$
Increasing the volume of the container will increase the amount of SO$_2$Cl$_2$
Increasing the temperature will increase the amount of SO$_2$Cl$_2$
Adding a catalyst will increase the amount of SO$_2$Cl$_2$

questions.question: A 1.0 L vessel initially contains only 6.0 mol of P and 6.0 mol of Q. At equilibrium 4.0 mol of R is present. What is $K_{eq}$ for $\text{P}(g)+\text{Q}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{R}(g)+\text{S}(g)$?

Creek water was suspected of containing a metal ion. Adding dilute HCl gave no reaction, adding H$_2$SO$_4$ gave a white precipitate, and a flame test gave a distinctive orange colour. Which ion could it be?
questions.answer: No chloride precipitate rules out lead; the sulfate precipitates; calcium gives an orange-red flame (barium is green).

questions.question: Four acids have these p$K_a$ values: W 4.87, X 4.82, Y 4.86, Z 4.85. What is their order of increasing acid strength?
questions.answer: Acid strength increases as p$K_a$ decreases.

questions.question: Complete combustion of a sample of a hydrocarbon produces 1.5 mol of CO$_2$ and 2.0 mol of water. What is its molecular formula?

What is the minimum volume of 0.500 mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid needed to react completely with 10.0 g of calcium carbonate? $$\text{CaCO}_3+\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\to\text{CaSO}_4+\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$$

Solutions of HCl and CH$_3$COOH of the same concentration (in equal volumes, in excess) reacted with separate 5.0 g samples of calcium carbonate until reaction was complete. Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: Acid strength affects the rate, not the stoichiometry. The same amount of CaCO$_3$ gives the same CO$_2$.
options: CH$_3$COOH reacted more slowly because it has a lower pH than HCl.
A smaller volume of CO$_2$ was produced with CH$_3$COOH than with HCl.
A greater volume of CO$_2$ was produced with CH$_3$COOH than with HCl.
The same volume of CO$_2$ was produced with both acids.

questions.question: Ammonia is a weak base with ionisation constant $K_b$. A relevant equation is $\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. Which is the correct expression for $K_b$ of ammonia?
questions.answer: $K_b$ refers to $\text{NH}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_4^++\text{OH}^-$; liquid water is omitted.

questions.question: 10 mL of 0.01 mol L$^{-1}$ HNO$_3$ is diluted with 90 mL of water. What is the pH of the resulting solution?
A base of concentration 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ is used to titrate 25 mL of an acid of concentration 0.01 mol L$^{-1}$. Which acid–base pair gives the highest pH at the equivalence point?
questions.answer: A strong base with a weak acid forms a basic salt.

questions.question: Compound X reacts with excess acidified potassium dichromate to form Y, which reacts with sodium carbonate to produce CO$_2$. What is a possible formula for X?
questions.answer: A primary alcohol is oxidised to a carboxylic acid.

questions.question: Excess BaCl$_2$ was added to a sample of Fe(NH$_4$)$_2$(SO$_4$)$_2$(aq), giving $5.02\times10^{-3}$ mol of BaSO$_4$. How many moles of sulfate ions and iron ions were in the sample?
questions.answer: Each mole of BaSO$_4$ is one mole of sulfate, and there are two sulfates per iron.

questions.question: Chromium(II) hydroxide has $K_{sp}=2.00\times10^{-16}$ at 25 °C. What is its molar solubility?

A student monitored fermentation, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\to2\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}+2\text{CO}_2$, by passing the gas into a flask of limewater and recording the flask's mass: day 1, 503.12 g; day 2, 505.68 g; day 3, 509.88 g; day 4, 512.16 g; day 5, 515.67 g. Which is closest to the mass of ethanol produced over the period?
questions.answer: CO$_2$ absorbed = 12.55 g = 0.2852 mol. Ethanol is 1 : 1 with CO$_2$: $0.2852\times46.07=13.1$ g.

questions.question: The mass spectrum of a molecule C$_3$H$_6$O shows major peaks at $m/z$ 58, 43, 29 and 15. Which is the most likely structure?
questions.answer: The peak at 29 (C$_2$H$_5^+$ or CHO$^+$) fits propanal.

questions.question: The three hydrogen environments of methyl propanoate are numbered 1, 2 and 3. Its high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum has peaks X (singlet), Y (quartet) and Z (triplet). Which environments give X, Y and Z respectively?
questions.answer: The OCH$_3$ (3) is a singlet, the CH$_2$ (2) a quartet and the CH$_3$ (1) a triplet.

questions.question: 150.0 mL of 0.100 mol L$^{-1}$ Pb(NO$_3$)$_2$ is added to 100.0 mL of 0.200 mol L$^{-1}$ NaCl. Predict mathematically whether a precipitate will form. ($K_{sp}$ PbCl$_2=1.70\times10^{-5}$)
Explain the processes involved in the dissolution of ionic compounds in water.
questions.answer: An ionic solid is a lattice of cations and anions held by strong electrostatic forces. Water is polar. Its partially negative oxygen atoms are attracted to cations and its partially positive hydrogen atoms to anions, forming ion–dipole attractions. Energy is needed to separate the ions (lattice energy) and to disrupt hydrogen bonds between water molecules; energy is released when ions are hydrated. Ions leave the lattice surrounded by shells of water molecules and disperse through the solution. Whether this is favourable depends on the enthalpy and entropy changes.

questions.question: Describe how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use solubility equilibria to remove toxicity from foods.
questions.answer: Cycad seeds contain a water-soluble toxin (cycasin). The seeds are cracked or ground, to increase surface area, and soaked for days in running water (leaching). The equilibrium is cycasin(s) $\rightleftharpoons$ cycasin(aq). Running water continually removes dissolved toxin, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts right and more toxin dissolves until very little remains and the food is safe to eat.

questions.question: Calculate the molar solubility of calcium carbonate at 25 °C. ($K_{sp}=3.36\times10^{-9}$)
Calculate the solubility of calcium carbonate ($K_{sp}=3.36\times10^{-9}$) in 0.150 mol L$^{-1}$ calcium chloride solution at 25 °C.
Explain why the solubility of calcium carbonate differs between water and calcium chloride solution.
questions.answer: This is the common ion effect. For $\text{CaCO}_3(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)$, the CaCl$_2$ solution already contains a high $[\text{Ca}^{2+}]$. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium lies further to the left (equivalently, $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]$ must be much smaller to keep $K_{sp}$ constant), so far less CaCO$_3$ dissolves than in pure water.

questions.question: Carbon monoxide reacts reversibly with chlorine to form phosgene, COCl$_2$. The concentration–time graph for the system in a closed container is shown. Identify what occurred at $t=32$ s.
questions.answer: The temperature was changed (decreased, since forming phosgene is exothermic): all concentrations change gradually with no sudden jump, and the equilibrium shifts towards COCl$_2$.

questions.question: Carbon monoxide reacts reversibly with chlorine to form phosgene, COCl$_2$. The concentration–time graph for the system in a closed container is shown. Explain the response of the system at $t=45$ s.
questions.answer: COCl$_2$ was added (its concentration jumps). By Le Chatelier's principle the system consumes some of it, shifting left for $\text{CO}+\text{Cl}_2\rightleftharpoons\text{COCl}_2$: [COCl$_2$] falls while [CO] and [Cl$_2$] rise until a new equilibrium is reached.

questions.question: Carbon monoxide reacts reversibly with chlorine to form phosgene, COCl$_2$. The concentration–time graph for the system in a closed container is shown. Calculate $K$ at $t=15$ s.

50.00 mL of 0.1000 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl was added to 25.00 mL of an ammonia-based cleaner. The excess HCl required an average of 21.50 mL of 0.1000 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH. Calculate the concentration of ammonia in the cleaner.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{HCl})_{added}=0.1000\times0.05000=5.000\times10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{HCl})_{excess}=n(\text{NaOH})=0.1000\times0.02150=2.150\times10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{NH}_3)=n(\text{HCl reacted})=2.850\times10^{-3}$ mol

$c(\text{NH}_3)=\dfrac{2.850\times10^{-3}}{0.02500}=0.1140$ mol L$^{-1}$

questions.question: What is a buffer?
questions.answer: A solution containing comparable amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

questions.question: A basic buffer is represented by $\text{A}^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{OH}^-(aq)+\text{HA}(aq)$. Explain how it responds to the addition of a strong base.
questions.answer: Adding base raises [OH⁻]. The equilibrium shifts left, with HA consuming most of the added OH⁻, so the pH changes only slightly.

questions.question: A basic buffer is represented by $\text{A}^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{OH}^-(aq)+\text{HA}(aq)$. Explain how it responds to the addition of a strong acid.
questions.answer: The added H₃O⁺ neutralises OH⁻, lowering [OH⁻]. The equilibrium shifts right (A⁻ reacts with water), replacing most of the OH⁻, so the pH changes only slightly.

questions.question: Outline the importance of a named buffer in a natural system.
questions.answer: The carbonic acid–hydrogencarbonate buffer in blood, $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{HCO}_3^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, keeps blood pH close to 7.4. This prevents acidosis or alkalosis, which would impair enzymes and cell function.

questions.question: 25.0 mL of 0.050 mol L$^{-1}$ KOH is added to 25.0 mL of 0.050 mol L$^{-1}$ H$_2$SO$_4$. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{H}^+)=2\times0.050\times0.0250=2.50\times10^{-3}$ mol; $n(\text{OH}^-)=1.25\times10^{-3}$ mol.

Excess $n(\text{H}^+)=1.25\times10^{-3}$ mol in 50.0 mL, so $[\text{H}^+]=0.025$ mol L$^{-1}$ and pH $=1.60$.

questions.question: Discuss the use of indicators in determining acidity.
questions.answer:
**For:** cheap, quick and simple; a few drops show whether a solution is acidic, neutral or basic, and a suitable indicator marks a titration end point accurately.

**Against:** each changes colour only over a narrow pH range and gives an approximate pH, not a value; judging colour is subjective; coloured or turbid samples mask the change; the indicator is itself a weak acid or base.

They suit rough testing and titrations, but a calibrated pH meter is better when an accurate value is needed.

questions.question: A conductance curve for the titration of HCl with NaOH is shown. Explain its shape.
questions.answer: Initially conductance is high because of the very mobile H⁺ ions. Added OH⁻ neutralises H⁺ to form water, replacing H⁺ with less mobile Na⁺, so conductance falls to a minimum at the equivalence point. Beyond it, excess mobile OH⁻ (and Na⁺) accumulate, so conductance rises.

questions.question: Draw (give) the polymer notation for polystyrene.
questions.answer: $$\left[-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)-\right]_n$$ (each repeat unit has a benzene ring on one backbone carbon).

questions.question: Outline a use of PVC, linking it to its properties.
questions.answer: Water pipes: PVC is rigid, strong, waterproof and resistant to chemical attack.

questions.question: Compare addition and condensation polymers.
questions.answer:
**Similarities:** both are long-chain molecules built from many small monomers joined by covalent bonds, with repeating units.

**Differences:**
- Addition monomers need a C=C double bond; condensation monomers need two reactive functional groups.
- Addition polymerisation gives only the polymer; condensation also releases a small molecule such as water.
- Addition polymers (polyethylene, PVC) usually have an all-carbon backbone; condensation polymers have links such as esters or amides (polyesters, nylon).

questions.question:
Boiling points (relative molecular mass, °C):

| Alkane | Mass | b.p. | Carboxylic acid | Mass | b.p. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Methane | 16 | −164 | Methanoic | 46 | 101 |
| Ethane | 30.1 | −87 | Ethanoic | 60.1 | 118 |
| Propane | 44.1 | −42 | Propanoic | 74.1 | 141 |
| Butane | 58.1 | −0.5 | Butanoic | 88.1 | 164 |
| Pentane | 72.1 | 36.1 | Pentanoic | 102.1 | 186 |
| Hexane | 86.2 | 68.7 | Hexanoic | 116.2 | 202 |

Explain the boiling point trends within and between these homologous series.
questions.answer:
Within each series boiling point rises with chain length: larger molecules have more electrons and surface area, so dispersion forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.

At similar mass, acids boil much higher than alkanes. Alkanes are non-polar and have only dispersion forces. Carboxylic acids have polar C=O and O–H bonds, giving dipole–dipole attractions and strong hydrogen bonds (often pairing as dimers), in addition to dispersion forces.

questions.question: Explain how soaps and detergents clean dirt off surfaces such as plates and clothes.
questions.answer: Soap and detergent particles have a long non-polar hydrocarbon tail (hydrophobic) and a polar or charged head (hydrophilic). The tails dissolve in grease through dispersion forces while the heads remain in the water (ion–dipole attractions). With agitation the grease is lifted off and enclosed in micelles, tails inwards and heads outwards. The micelles repel one another, stay suspended as an emulsion and are rinsed away. Surfactants also lower surface tension, helping water wet the surface.

questions.question: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of ethanol with propanoic acid.
questions.answer: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}(l)+\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}(l)\ \underset{\text{heat}}{\overset{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4}{\rightleftharpoons}}\ \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3(l)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

questions.question: Name the ester formed when ethanol reacts with propanoic acid.
questions.answer: Ethyl propanoate.

questions.question: Justify the use of refluxing in esterification.
questions.answer: Esterification is slow at room temperature, so the mixture is heated to increase the rate and reach equilibrium sooner. The reactants and ester are volatile and flammable. A vertical condenser condenses the vapours and returns them to the flask, so material is not lost and yield is maintained while heating for a long time. The open top prevents pressure building up.

questions.question: How are ions present in the environment identified and measured?
questions.answer:
**Identification**
- Precipitation tests: selective reagents form characteristic precipitates (e.g. Ag⁺ confirms Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ by colour; Ba²⁺ confirms SO₄²⁻).
- Complexation: formation or dissolving of coloured or soluble complexes (e.g. SCN⁻ gives blood red with Fe³⁺; Cu²⁺ gives deep blue with excess NH₃).
- Flame tests: characteristic colours (Ba²⁺ green, Ca²⁺ orange-red, Cu²⁺ blue-green).

**Measurement**
- Gravimetric analysis: precipitate the ion, filter, dry and weigh, then use stoichiometry.
- Precipitation titration: e.g. Cl⁻ titrated with standard AgNO₃ with a chromate indicator (Mohr method).
- Colourimetry and UV–visible spectrophotometry: absorbance of a coloured species is proportional to concentration (Beer–Lambert law), read from a calibration curve.
- Atomic absorption spectroscopy: atoms in a flame absorb light from a lamp of the same element; the absorbance, compared with standards, measures trace metal ions.

Qualitative tests show what is present; the instrumental methods are most sensitive for low concentrations.

questions.question: For a named ion, explain why it is important to monitor its presence in the environment.
questions.answer: Phosphate enters waterways from fertilisers and detergents. In excess it causes eutrophication: algae bloom, block light and die; bacteria decomposing them consume dissolved oxygen, killing fish and other aquatic life, and some blooms are toxic. Monitoring detects rising levels early so sources can be controlled and ecosystems and water supplies protected.

questions.question: Compound X is 68.11% C, 13.74% H and 18.15% O by mass. Show that its empirical formula is C$_5$H$_{12}$O.
Compound X has empirical formula C$_5$H$_{12}$O. Its mass, infrared, ¹³C NMR and ¹H NMR spectra are shown. Analyse all four spectra to deduce the identity of X.
questions.answer:
**Mass spectrum:** M⁺ = 88, equal to the empirical formula mass, so the molecular formula is C$_5$H$_{12}$O. The peak at 73 is loss of CH$_3$ (15); the base peak at 59 is loss of C$_2$H$_5$ (29), giving (CH$_3$)$_2$COH⁺.

**IR:** a broad absorption near 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ shows an alcohol O–H; C–H stretches near 2850–3000 cm⁻¹; no C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹.

**¹³C NMR:** four signals for five carbons, so two carbons are equivalent. The signal near 71 ppm is a carbon bonded to O; the others (about 37, 29 and 9 ppm) are alkyl carbons, the tall one near 29 ppm fitting two equivalent CH$_3$.

**¹H NMR:** a triplet (3H, ≈0.9 ppm, CH$_3$ next to CH$_2$), a large singlet (6H, ≈1.2 ppm, two CH$_3$ on a carbon with no H), a quartet (2H, ≈1.5 ppm, CH$_2$ next to CH$_3$) and a small singlet (1H, ≈1.9 ppm, OH).

**X is 2-methylbutan-2-ol,** CH$_3$CH$_2$C(CH$_3$)$_2$OH.

*Note: the paper lists the ¹H splitting from right to left as quartet, singlet, triplet, singlet. It should be triplet, singlet, quartet, singlet.*
